background_notes.fact: If u is C^2 on R^n x (0,infinity), then at every (x,t), partial_t |u_t|^2=2 u_t dot u_tt, and partial_t |partial_{x_j}u|^2=2 partial_{x_j}u dot partial_{x_j}u_t. Hence the finite sum defining e has exactly the pointwise derivative asserted in F001.

grounds.reason: n and m are positive finite integers, so all coordinate sums are finite.
Joint C-infinity regularity supplies C^2 regularity and continuous mixed partials on an open domain.
u_tt is the second time derivative.
e is the indicated finite sum of Euclidean squares.

background_notes.justification: Expand each squared norm as the finite sum of squares of scalar components and differentiate by the scalar product rule. Continuous second mixed partials commute: the rectangle-increment identity, divided by the side lengths, gives the same limit for either order by continuity of the mixed partials. Apply this to each component and each spatial coordinate. This verifies the product and mixed-derivative rules in their actual domains without any equation of motion.

background_notes.justification: A finite product of closed bounded real intervals is compact. Its continuous image under |e_t| is compact in R, hence bounded, so a nonnegative bound exists. background_notes.fact: If Q is a Borel measurable set of finite Lebesgue measure and B>=0 is finite, then b(y)=B 1_Q(y) is absolutely integrable and integral |b|=B mu(Q)<infinity.

background_notes.justification: The characteristic function of a measurable set is a measurable simple function; its integral is the measure of that set. Scaling by B gives absolute integral B mu(Q). This is exactly the common bound required by M001.

background_notes.fact: For each fixed k under L2, Fseq(k):R^n->R is continuous and therefore mu-almost everywhere strongly measurable for spatial Lebesgue measure.

background_notes.justification: Subtraction and multiplication by a constant preserve continuity, so Fseq(k) is Borel measurable. Real-valued Borel functions are strongly measurable because their separable codomain permits finite simple-function approximations obtained by truncating the range and subdividing it into rational intervals. These approximations converge pointwise; thus strong measurability, and in particular its almost everywhere version for mu, holds.
